title: Identifying Website Maintenance Clues During Prospecting
dek: Learn how to spot website maintenance clues during prospecting by reading footers, copyright years, and contact forms without jumping to conclusions.
intro_paragraphs: Prospecting usually starts with incomplete information. You have a business name, maybe a phone number, a directory listing, and a website. The website is often the richest public artifact available, because it is where a business shows what it sells and how it wants to be contacted. Sometimes it also shows how long it has been since anyone touched the site.

That last part is where useful clues live. During prospecting, your job is not to diagnose a business or declare its website neglected. Your job is to observe specific, checkable details and record them accurately. The difference matters: guessing at causes leads to claims you cannot support.

body_sections.heading: What Counts as a Maintenance Clue
paragraphs: A maintenance clue is any observable detail on a live website that hints at how recently, how consistently, or how carefully someone has been tending to it.
Three properties make a clue useful:
Observable. You can point at it. "The footer says 2018" is observable. "The owner does not care" is not.
Verifiable. Someone else can look at the same page and see the same thing.
Time-bounded. It hints at a window, not a verdict. A copyright year gives you a year. A blog post gives you a date. A broken link tells you only that it is broken now.
Collect clues in groups. One clue is noise. Three clues pointing the same direction is a pattern worth noting, and even a pattern is a hypothesis, not a fact.

body_sections.heading: Looking for Recent Copyright or Footer Updates
paragraphs: The footer is often overlooked, which makes it informative. It is also commonly generated by a template and forgotten.

body_sections.heading: What the footer contains
paragraphs: Before reading anything into it, inventory it. A typical footer holds:
Each is a separate observation. Do not collapse them into one impression.
bullets: A copyright line, sometimes with a year or year range
The business name, and sometimes a legal entity name
A physical address and phone number
Links to privacy policies, terms, or accessibility statements
Social media icons
A credit line, such as "Site by [agency]" or a platform name

body_sections.heading: Reading year ranges carefully
paragraphs: A footer that reads "© 2014-2021" may mean someone edited that line in 2021, or that a script generated the year automatically. A footer that reads "© 2016" may mean the line was last edited manually in 2016, or that the site uses a static footer nobody has refreshed. It does not establish when the site was last maintained.

Some content management systems and themes render the current year with a snippet, so a site can display the current year while little else has changed. A current copyright year is weak evidence of activity, and a stale one is weak evidence of inactivity. Neither is conclusive on its own.
In most jurisdictions, copyright notices are not legally required for protection to exist. A stale year is a maintenance signal, not evidence of a legal problem.

body_sections.heading: Footer details worth recording
paragraphs: Inconsistency between a footer and a business listing is concrete and easy to confirm with the owner.
bullets: Does the phone number match directory listings?
Does the address match, including suite numbers?
Do social icons lead to profiles that exist and have recent posts?
Do legal pages load, or do they return errors?
Is there an agency credit, and does that agency still exist?

body_sections.heading: Recognizing Active or Stagnant Contact Forms
paragraphs: Contact forms are where maintenance and inquiries meet. A form that is broken or confusing can block some inquiries, though the impact depends on traffic, alternatives, and whether anyone monitors responses.

body_sections.heading: Functional signals
paragraphs: You can learn a lot without submitting anything:

A mailto: action is notable. It hands off to the visitor's email client, which may be inconvenient or fail for some users, especially those relying on browser-based webmail. Behavior varies by browser, email client, and user setup. It is not automatically broken, but it can be fragile.

You generally should not submit test messages to a prospect's form. If you do, use a clearly identified address, send one message, and expect that a real person may read it. Structural signals can often be checked without submission.
bullets: Does the form render correctly, with all fields visible?
Does it use client-side validation, or does it accept anything?
Is there an anti-spam mechanism, such as a CAPTCHA or a honeypot field?
What does the form post to? A third-party endpoint, a plugin route, or a mailto: link?

body_sections.heading: Structural signals
paragraphs: The fields themselves carry date information. Ask what a form built today would look like, then compare:

None of these proves the form is unmaintained. A fax field in an industry that still uses fax may be reasonable. But a cluster of outdated fields is a fair indication that nobody has reviewed the form recently.
bullets: Does it ask for a fax number?
Does it include a "Home phone" field alongside a mobile field?
Does a "How did you hear about us?" dropdown list channels that no longer exist?
Does it collect personal data with no consent checkbox or privacy link nearby?

body_sections.heading: What stagnation tends to look like
bullets: The form posts to a mailto: link
There is no confirmation message or thank you page after submission
Required fields are missing, so submissions may arrive incomplete
There is no obvious way to tell whether a submission was received
The form is the only contact option, with no phone or email alternative

body_sections.heading: What activity tends to look like
paragraphs: Treat these as observations too. A business can have a functional form and still be a poor fit, and a business with an old form can be thriving.
bullets: A hosted form handler or a maintained plugin
A thank you page, which can be consistent with conversion tracking, though it does not prove tracking is configured
A scheduling widget embedded alongside the form
Multiple contact paths that agree with each other
A privacy notice near the submit button

body_sections.heading: Other Observable Signals
paragraphs: The footer and contact form are high-yield areas, but a few other checks take seconds each.

body_sections.heading: Content freshness
paragraphs: Look for dated content: blog posts, news items, event listings, seasonal banners. An events page advertising a fundraiser that has passed is a concrete, dated observation. A holiday banner still visible in July is another.

body_sections.heading: Technical hygiene
paragraphs: Page speed is worth checking, but be careful. Results vary by connection, device, and time of day, so a single measurement is not a stable claim about site quality.
bullets: Broken images or missing stylesheets
Links that return errors, especially in navigation
Mixed content warnings, where a secure page loads insecure assets
A missing viewport meta tag, which usually means the layout was not built for phones
An outdated JavaScript library named in the page source

body_sections.heading: Platform and security signals
paragraphs: Page source often reveals a generator tag naming a platform and version. An old version number is a clue about update cadence, though not proof that anything is wrong. An expired or mismatched TLS certificate, which browsers flag loudly, is a more serious and more verifiable observation.

body_sections.heading: Keeping Observations Separate From Assumptions
paragraphs: For each clue, write down what you saw, then what it might mean, then resist treating the second as the first.
Example: You observe that the footer copyright reads 2018, the contact form posts to a mailto: link, and two footer links return errors. Those are three observations.
What they might mean: the site has not received routine maintenance in some time. What they do not mean: the business is failing, the owner does not care, or the business has no budget.

There is also a correlation trap. A site with a stale footer may also rank poorly, load slowly, or have thin content. It is tempting to describe one as the cause of another. In practice, several issues can share a common source, such as a low level of attention to the web presence overall. That shared source is a hypothesis, not a finding.

body_sections.heading: Turning Clues Into Prospect Notes
paragraphs: Record evidence rather than conclusions. Compare these two notes:
Weak: "Site is neglected."
Useful: "Footer copyright shows 2018. Contact form posts to a mailto: link with no confirmation step. Two footer links return errors. Phone number in footer differs from the listing."
The second note can be read aloud without insulting anyone, and it gives the owner something specific to check. Every item is something you can demonstrate.
If you keep a scoring system, score evidence categories: last observable update, contact path integrity, technical hygiene, and consistency with business listings. Rate each on what you actually saw.

body_sections.heading: A Short Prospecting Checklist
paragraphs: The results produce notes you can actually use. How long the checklist takes will vary by site and by how thorough you are.
bullets: Footer copyright year or range
Footer contact details compared against directory listings
Footer and navigation links tested for errors
Contact form handler and endpoint
Contact form fields reviewed for outdated prompts
Presence of a confirmation or thank you step
Most recent dated content on the site
Seasonal or event content that has passed
Secure connection and certificate status
Mobile rendering and viewport tag
Social profile links that resolve

body_sections.heading: Where to Go From Here
paragraphs: Maintenance clues are one input into prospecting, not the whole picture. Once you have a stack of observations, the next step is deciding which ones map to work you can offer and which prospects are worth contacting first. For that, review how to find website and SEO opportunities in a local lead list.
The habit worth building is simple: look, write down what you see, and hold the interpretation loosely until the owner confirms it.
